sections.h2: Who to call about Fleming County property tax
sections.html:
Two offices on Court Square carry most of the load, and a third takes over when a bill goes bad. The PVA answers value questions at 606-845-1401 with the office open 8 to 4:30 on weekdays. The sheriff bills and collects at 201 Court Square in Flemingsburg. Phones there are answered at 606-845-4701 (press 1) from 8 until 4:30, Monday to Friday. Once a bill is delinquent, the county clerk handles it.

The PVA appraises property at fair cash value, maintains tax maps and ownership records and processes exemptions. It does not write laws or set rates. Rates come from the fiscal court, city councils, the school board and other districts. The fiscal court meets at the courthouse, 100 Court Square, on the second Tuesday of every month at 9 a.m. Eastern.

Every property gets a visit from the PVA or a deputy at least once every four years, and the outside of a building can be measured with or without the owner present. Send the PVA any new mailing address in writing so notices do not go astray.

sections.h2: Tax year, due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Fleming follows the standard Kentucky calendar, which opens October 1. Statements usually leave the sheriff's office near the end of September. A missing bill changes nothing about the debt, so owners without one should phone 606-845-4701 and ask for the balance, or use the sheriff's online tax record search.

The discount ends every November 1. From then through December 31 the plain bill amount is due. Waiting until February raises the cost by a fifth.

  • At the counter, pay with cash, a money order, or a check made out to the Fleming County Sheriff.
  • Card payments, in person or by phone, carry a 2.5 percent service charge.
  • Mailed payments need a postmark dated on or before the due date.
  • A drop box at the sheriff's door stays open at all hours and is emptied at 8 each morning under camera watch.

Start with the PVA, because the board will not hear anyone who skipped that step. Every May, starting on the first Monday, the roll sits open to inspection for thirteen days. Holding a conference in that period preserves your right to file with the county clerk until the next business day after inspection ends. If inspection runs from May 3 to May 17, for instance, the clerk must have the paper by the close of May 18.

The local board of assessment appeals then sits 25 to 35 days afterward. Bring paper. The board turns down any appeal lacking insurance policies, building costs, sale listings or similar proof.

  • The PVA owes you an explanation of how the value was reached at the conference, and must write down the outcome.
  • A paid representative has to come from a profession on the state's list, among them attorneys, CPAs and certified appraisers, and must bring your signed authorization.
  • Hearings may be audio-recorded by the taxpayer.

The sheriff will redirect any value complaint to the PVA. Filing and then missing the hearing closes the door to the Kentucky Claims Commission.

For a qualifying owner it is worth claiming. On the 2025 and 2026 rolls the state takes $49,100 off the home's assessed value, and tax is figured on the remainder. The typical owner-occupied house in the county is valued at $134,700, so the deduction removes a large slice of a typical assessment.

The PVA takes the form. Owners show their age with a birth certificate, license, passport or comparable record. Total disability must be certified by a federal agency or a retirement system, with benefits paid across the entire year, and most such claims have to be re-filed each year. The yearly re-filing does not apply to owners with service-connected military disabilities or those ruled permanently and totally disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

When a lender pays from escrow, the owner is still expected to confirm the payment arrived on time. Check the sheriff's record search after the discount period closes.

The tax follows ownership, and the sheriff will talk through proration for any buyer or seller who calls with a closing date. Under KRS 134.015 the owner personally owes the tax from the assessment date, and under KRS 134.420 a lien on an unpaid parcel can stay for 11 years after a sale. A sensible order of events: get the balance from the sheriff before listing, then have the closing agent settle the year's bill.

When the sheriff's office closes on April 15, whatever is unpaid goes to the Fleming County Clerk under KRS 134.122. Expect interest of 1 percent monthly, plus commissions and a lien fee, and two letters from the county attorney. The clerk's tax sale follows once 90 to 135 days have gone by.

The deed also carries a state transfer tax, which the seller pays. The seller owes $0.50 for each $500 of price, rounding a partial block up.

If you are listing soon, ask the sheriff whether the current bill has been paid and keep the receipt. A buyer's title company will look for it, and a paid-up record shortens the closing checklist.

Ask the clerk's office in Flemingsburg for a payoff on any transferred bill, and tell the PVA about a new mailing address after closing. At the closing table, the title agent will want the paid receipt for the current year or a payoff letter, so request one from the sheriff ahead of time.

sections.h2: Fleming County housing and the local market
sections.html:
Flemingsburg is the county seat and Ewing is the second city. Population is 15,787, and owners live in 74.8 percent of housing, across 5,859 households. Typical home value is $134,700 and typical monthly rent is $715. No building permits were issued in 2025.

Without new construction, nearly every buyer is shopping among older houses, so condition matters. A seller who owes taxes or faces repairs can weigh the cost of fixing up a listing against an as-is cash offer. Selling for cash skips the appraisal, loan approval and repair requests. Any tax balance comes out of the proceeds at closing. Before listing, make a short folder with the latest tax bill, the sheriff's payoff figure and the deed, so a buyer or title agent can move quickly.

faqs.q: When do Fleming County tax bills arrive?
faqs.a: Bills usually mail late in September, and the 2 percent discount begins October 1. An owner who has no bill by then can call 606-845-4701 and press 1.

faqs.q: How much extra does a late Fleming County payment cost?
faqs.a: January adds 5 percent. Between February 1 and April 15 the total climbs to 121 percent, and whatever is still open afterward is turned over to the county clerk.

faqs.q: Where is the Fleming County Sheriff's tax counter?
faqs.a: Find it at 201 Court Square in Flemingsburg, weekdays 8 to 4:30. The entrance drop box accepts payments at any hour.

faqs.q: Who changes a Fleming County property value?
faqs.a: Only the PVA, at 606-845-1401. The sheriff has no say over assessments, and an appeal must be preceded by a PVA conference.

faqs.q: Who gets the Fleming County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: Owners who live in the home and are 65 or older or totally disabled. The exemption takes $49,100 off the value on the 2025 and 2026 rolls.
